strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely important and underexplored problem: predicting, before expensive training, whether a given unsupervised pretext task will benefit a downstream target task. The motivation that pretext-task selection is currently heuristic is well argued.

The unifying framing of SSL and neuro-symbolic learning as both relying on 'probabilistic knowledge' (knowledge that holds with some probability) is an interesting conceptual contribution, and the three-factor decomposition (learnability, reliability, completeness) offers an intuitive vocabulary for analyzing why pretext tasks succeed or fail, connecting to known phenomena such as the NeSy shortcut problem.

The empirical protocol is unusual and potentially useful: a benchmark of 115 pretext-task variants (11 augmentation families at varying strengths) with paired 'cheap prediction' vs. 'full training' outcomes on both semi-supervised and self-supervised pipelines, reporting Pearson correlations of 0.72-0.82 using only 5 labeled and 50 unlabeled samples per class for estimation.

The proposed estimation procedure is inexpensive and self-contained, and the paper is upfront that the theoretical indicators are approximated via a small supervised 'oracle' model rather than a true oracle.
weaknesses: The theoretical development is not rigorous despite claims of 'rigorous theoretical analysis.' Equations 1-8 contain no stated theorems, assumptions, or proofs. Eq. (1) is a heuristic Bayesian decomposition asserted without derivation; the key inequality (4) and the chain of inequalities leading to (8) are stated without proof or conditions under which they hold. The indicator-event notation (e.g., I(f(x), K_A |≠ True), the definitions in Eqs. 5 and 7) is imprecise, and it is unclear whether R_Target ≤ 1-(1-R_Unlearnable)(1-R_Unreliable)(1-R_Incomplete) actually holds for a trained f versus being a definitional decomposition.

There is a fundamental gap between the theory and the experimental claim: the bound characterizes generalization error of a model f on the target task as a function of its errors on the pretext task, but the paper's headline claim is that performance after full-scale SSL training can be predicted from cheap pre-training estimates. No theoretical argument connects the bound to post-SSL-training performance; the validation is purely correlational.

Potential circularity in the estimation method: both the reliability estimate (Eq. 14) and the completeness estimate (Eq. 16) use f̂_Target, a supervised model trained on the same small labeled set, as a stand-in for ground truth. The 'predicted performance' may therefore largely track the quality of this tiny supervised model and the augmentation strength, rather than genuinely measuring knowledge reliability/completeness. No ablation isolates the contribution of each of the three factors, and no baselines are compared (e.g., simply predicting performance from augmentation strength, from pretext training loss alone, or from the small supervised model's test accuracy).

The experimental setup is weak by current standards: ViT-B trained for only 5 epochs with batch size 64 on CIFAR-10/100, yielding actual test accuracies of roughly 15-60%, far below what proper SSL/semi-supervised methods achieve. It is unclear whether conclusions transfer to realistic training regimes, larger label budgets, or datasets beyond CIFAR.

The evaluation metric (correlation across tasks) does not directly test the practical claim of 'cost-effective task selection.' The decisive question - whether ranking tasks by predicted performance and picking the top one yields near-optimal actual performance - is never evaluated, nor are rank-based metrics (e.g., Spearman correlation, regret of the selected task) reported.

Presentation quality is below bar for a main-track submission: repeated typos ('the the comparison'), broken references (Huang et al. and Jia et al. cited with '????' year/venue), crowded and hard-to-read scatter figures, no proofs or derivations in an appendix, and only one table describing the task benchmark. Reproducibility is undermined: no code release is mentioned and many implementation details (e.g., how consistency is thresholded to decide '(x, K) |= True', the prototype alignment details) are underspecified.

Novelty relative to prior theoretical work on pretext-task/target-task relationships (Lee et al. 2021; Teng, Huang, and He 2022, which the authors themselves cite) is not clearly delineated; the paper does not explain what its three-factor bound adds over existing generalization analyses beyond the NeSy framing.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely useful and underexplored problem: predicting, before expensive training, whether a given unsupervised pretext task will benefit a downstream target task.
The three-factor framing (learnability, reliability, completeness) is intuitive and provides a common vocabulary that connects SSL assumptions to the NeSy shortcut/incomplete-knowledge literature.

The proposed low-cost estimation pipeline (training on tiny labeled/unlabeled subsets to estimate the three indicators) is practically motivated, and the benchmark of 115 pretext-task variants is a non-trivial empirical effort.

The experimental design—comparing cheaply estimated performance against full semi-supervised/self-supervised training across many pretext tasks—is the right kind of validation to attempt for this problem.
weaknesses: The 'theoretical derivation' is not rigorous. Equations (2)–(8) are essentially a tautological partition of the data into disjoint events (unlearnable / learnable-but-unreliable / learnable-reliable-but-incomplete); no formal theorem, proof, or assumption set is given, despite claims of a 'generalization error bound'. Eq. (8) silently mixes population quantities R with undefined estimates R̂, and the notation ((x, K) |= True) used as an event inside probabilities in Eq. (1) is informal and never precisely defined.

The central empirical claim is vulnerable to a fundamental confound that is never addressed: all 115 'pretext tasks' are parameter sweeps of 11 augmentation strengths. Both the predicted performance and the actual performance plausibly degrade monotonically with augmentation severity, so a moderate correlation (Pearson 0.72–0.82) may simply reflect task difficulty, not the validity of the three-factor theory. There is no baseline comparison (e.g., ranking pretext tasks by pretext training loss alone, or by augmentation strength) that would show the three indicators add predictive value over trivial alternatives.

There is circularity in the estimation procedure: reliability and completeness are estimated using f̂Target, a model trained on only 5 labels per class, as a pseudo-oracle—yet the quantity being predicted is precisely how well a model performs on the target task. The prediction and the pseudo-oracle are entangled, and the paper offers no analysis or ablation (e.g., varying the number of labeled samples) to show the estimates are meaningful rather than self-fulfilling.

The experimental setup is too weak to support the claims: ViT-B trained for only 5 epochs with batch size 64 and MSE loss is far from representative of modern semi-/self-supervised practice; only CIFAR-10/100 are used; only consistency-type pretext knowledge is considered (despite claims of unifying NeSy and SSL theory); no error bars, seeds, or variance analysis are reported; and the paper never demonstrates that using the method for actual task selection yields better downstream models than heuristic selection—the motivating use case.

The claimed unification of NeSy and SSL theory is overclaimed. The formalism never uses any neuro-symbolic machinery; 'knowledge K' reduces to the augmentation-invariance assumption, and the NeSy connection is limited to loose discussion of shortcuts.

Presentation quality is below bar for a main-track paper: numerous typos ('the the comparison'), broken references (Huang et al. ????; Jia et al. ????), one citation (Mao et al. 2019) used for two different categories, inconsistent hat notation across Eqs. (6)–(8), unreadable scatter plots with overlapping point labels, and no limitations section, no reproducibility statement, and no code release.

Figures 1–4 show visibly clustered points and outliers; correlations of 0.72–0.79 on single runs, without confidence intervals or a causal/interventional experiment (e.g., deliberately corrupting knowledge reliability and checking the predicted degradation), are insufficient to 'confirm the validity of the theory' as claimed.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored problem: predicting, before costly large-scale training, whether an unsupervised pretext task will benefit a downstream target task. The motivation that pretext task selection is currently heuristic is convincing and well documented in the related work.

The conceptual unification of semi-supervised learning, self-supervised learning, and neuro-symbolic learning under a single probabilistic-knowledge framework (learnability, reliability, completeness) is an interesting and potentially influential reframing, connecting the NeSy shortcut literature to pretext task misalignment in SSL.

The proposed decomposition is operationalizable at low cost, and the authors construct a benchmark of 115 pretext tasks (augmentation families with varying strengths) to evaluate the prediction procedure, which is a useful experimental artifact.

The empirical observation that performance estimated from only ~5 labeled and ~50 unlabeled samples per class correlates with full-scale training outcomes (Pearson r of 0.72-0.82 across four settings) is a nontrivial and practically relevant finding.
weaknesses: The theoretical derivation is not rigorous despite claims of 'rigorous theoretical analysis.' Equation (1) is asserted rather than proven, and it does not follow from standard probability rules as written (the conditional terms are ill-defined as events rather than random variables). The step from Equations (6)-(7) to Equation (8), including the sudden appearance of hatted quantities and the final equality, is unjustified. No formal proofs are provided, and the relationships between the stated inequalities and the eventual product-form estimate (Equation 17) are heuristic.

There is a fundamental gap between the theory and the estimation procedure that is not addressed: the theory concerns generalization errors of the final model, but the estimates use training errors of models fit on tiny data (e.g., a ViT-B trained for 5 epochs on 500 samples). The paper provides no argument for why these estimates should predict performance after large-scale training, other than the observed correlation itself.

The reliability and completeness estimates rely on a weak 'oracle' f̂_Target trained on only 5 labeled samples per class, which is likely near-random on CIFAR-100. This raises a serious confound: the predictions may largely reflect the biases and errors of this weak proxy model rather than properties of the pretext task. No analysis isolates this effect.

Critical ablations are missing. The paper does not test whether the full three-factor product adds value over a single indicator (e.g., correlating pretext task training loss alone with downstream performance), which would establish whether the decomposition is necessary or whether any monotone difficulty proxy achieves similar correlation. There are also no baselines from existing transferability-estimation methods (e.g., LogME, linear-probe speedup), which directly target the same problem.

The experimental scope is narrow: only CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100, a single architecture, and pretext tasks restricted to augmentation-strength variations of one consistency prior. The 'full' training regime (ViT-B, batch 64, 5 epochs, Adam) is far from realistic semi/self-supervised practice, limiting external validity of the central claim. The moderate correlations (0.72-0.82) are reported without confidence intervals, statistical significance tests, or repetition.

The claimed practical benefit (pretext task selection) is never actually demonstrated: the paper reports correlations but never shows that the method selects better tasks than heuristic alternatives, nor quantifies cost savings concretely.

Presentation issues are significant: scatter plots (Figures 1-4) are cluttered and largely unreadable due to overlapping text labels; notation such as 'f(x), K_A |= True' is nonstandard and inconsistently used; definitions in Equations (3), (5), (7) silently switch distributions and conditions; there are broken citations ('????' for Huang et al. and Jia et al.), grammatical errors, and Equation (2)/(3) mix marginal and joint events. No code or supplementary material appears to be provided, hurting reproducibility.

The framing that this work 'changes the status quo' and shifts selection 'from heuristic-based to theory-based' is overclaimed relative to the evidence, which supports only a modest correlation in a restricted setting.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and underexplored problem: estimating, at low cost, whether an unsupervised pretext task will benefit a downstream target task before full training and validation. This could meaningfully reduce trial-and-error cost in SSL pipelines.

The framing via knowledge-integrated (NeSy) learning—treating SSL assumptions as probabilistically reliable knowledge and decomposing benefit into learnability, reliability, and completeness—is a conceptually interesting unification, and the connection to the shortcut/incompleteness problem in NeSy is a genuinely novel angle.

The empirical study is extensive: a benchmark of 115 pretext task configurations, three datasets (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet-200), ablations over the three indicators (Tables 2-3), and robustness checks across algorithms (MeanTeacher, UDA, FixMatch, SimCLR, MoCo, BYOL, DINO), backbones (ViT-B, ResNet-50), data distribution (Office-31), data scale, and hyperparameters.
A cost comparison (Table 4) quantifies the claimed efficiency gain (~29.6s vs. ~1500-1650s and far less labeled data), and the appendix includes statistical testing of the correlation claims.
The ablation results plausibly support that each of the three indicators adds signal: e.g., self-supervised correlation rises from 0.224 (learnability only) to 0.820 (all three).
weaknesses: The central 'rigorous derivation' is not rigorous. Equation (1) is presented as a factorization of p(y|x), but the product p[(x,KA)|=True|x]·p[(y,KA)|=True|...]·p[y|...] is a chain-rule expansion of the joint event, which equals p(y|x) only when the knowledge holds with probability one; the general case is never formally established. Equations (4), (6), and (8) are presented as bounds ('R_target ≤ ...') but no theorems, assumptions, or proofs are given—the transitions are justified narratively ('It thus follows that', 'This leads to the following formulation'). For a paper whose headline claim is a theory-based estimator, this is a major soundness gap.

The empirical estimates involve multiple uncontrolled approximations that are never analyzed: learnability is estimated from training error on 5-epoch small-data runs (which conflates optimization with true generalization), reliability relies on pseudo-labels from a supervised model trained with only 5 labels per class (a circularity the paper acknowledges but does not quantify), and completeness uses a heuristic prototype alignment (Eq. 16) whose sensitivity is not studied. No error bars, confidence intervals, or seed variance are reported for any estimate or correlation.

The reported correlations are weaker than the claims. Pearson correlations of 0.675/0.678 (ImageNet-200), 0.453 (MoCo), 0.478 (ResNet-50 semi-supervised), and 0.603 (BYOL) do not support the repeated assertion that estimated and actual performance are 'highly correlated.' The scatter plots show substantial deviation and a strongly bimodal actual-performance structure, for which Pearson correlation may overstate utility; the hypothesis test against a critical r of 0.226 is a very weak evidentiary bar—statistical significance of a nonzero correlation does not establish useful predictive accuracy.

The benchmark is narrow: all 115 'pretext tasks' are variations of 11 augmentation-based consistency transformations. The framework is claimed to be general for SSL pretext tasks, but heterogeneous pretext families (rotation prediction, jigsaw, masked modeling, etc.—which the paper itself cites) are never tested, so the scope of the learnability/reliability/completeness decomposition over arbitrary assumptions remains unverified.

Reproducibility concerns: no code or benchmark release is mentioned; several key details (e.g., how the consistency indicator is thresholded for the indicator function in Eq. 10, exactly how the pseudo-oracle f̂_target interacts with the assumption check) are underspecified. There are also broken cross-references ('??' in the appendix), typos ('reache', 'excepted labeled ones'), and an incorrect/odd citation of ViT (attributed to 'Dosoviskiy 2020' with a single author) and Pearson (1895), suggesting insufficient polish.

The practical workflow requires training both a pretext model and a supervised target model on curated labeled data before estimation; the paper does not discuss how sensitive the estimates are to the quality of f̂_target, nor compare against simpler baselines (e.g., correlation of pretext loss alone, linear-probe cost, or existing transferability-estimation methods such as LEEP/logme-style scores cited only in passing), so the relative merit of the three-indicator scheme is unclear.

Limitations are not honestly discussed: the conclusion and impact statement do not acknowledge the moderate correlations, the restriction to augmentation-type assumptions, or the reliance on labeled data for the oracle surrogate.

strengths: The core question—predicting whether a pretext task will help a target task before expensive full-scale SSL training—is practically relevant and underexplored.

The conceptual decomposition of SSL benefit into assumption learnability, reliability, and completeness is a novel framing, and the attempt to connect SSL assumptions with knowledge-integrated/neuro-symbolic theory is an interesting angle.

The empirical effort is substantial: a 115-task benchmark (11 augmentation operations × strength levels), three image datasets, ablations over the three indicators, and robustness checks across algorithms (MeanTeacher, UDA, FixMatch, SimCLR, MoCo, BYOL, DINO), backbones (ViT-B, ResNet-50), distributions (Office-31), data scales, and hyperparameters.
The cost comparison (Table 4) quantifies the claimed ~50x time savings of estimation versus full training and validation, and hypothesis testing is used to assess significance of the correlations.
weaknesses: The theoretical derivation is loose and does not support the central claims. Eq. (1) is presented without proof, and the final bound (Eq. 8), R_target ≤ 1-(1-R_unlearnable)(1-R_unreliable)(1-R_incomplete), implicitly assumes independence between the three error events. These quantities are not independent (e.g., R_unlearnable is defined over f's fit to the pretext task while R_unreliable is a property of the data distribution), and neither the inequality direction nor the multiplicative factorization is rigorously justified. No formal theorem, proof, or statement of assumptions is provided; calling this 'rigorous derivation' oversells heuristic decomposition.

The framework is circular in key places. Learnability is estimated via training error after training on the pretext task—so the method already requires pretext training, undermining the 'estimate before training' narrative. Reliability and completeness both rely on pseudo-labels from f_target trained on only 5 labels per class, which in such low-label regimes is extremely weak; the quality of these surrogate labels is never assessed, and estimation errors propagate through all three indicators.

A crucial baseline is missing: with the same small labeled set used by the method, a natural competitor is to simply train a small model with the pretext task and evaluate on the labeled set (or use standard transferability estimation metrics such as LEEP/LogME from a pretext-trained model). The paper cites transferability evaluation (Kornblith et al. 2019) but does not compare against any such approach, so it is impossible to judge whether the three-factor decomposition adds value over simpler alternatives.

The claimed benchmark diversity is overstated: all 115 'pretext tasks' are variations of the same augmentation-invariance family (11 operations × strengths). The paper never tests genuinely heterogeneous pretext tasks (e.g., rotation prediction, jigsaw, masked modeling), so the generalization of the theory beyond invariance assumptions remains unverified. Moreover, the 'self-supervised' setting differs from the 'semi-supervised' setting only in training order under a unified MSE consistency loss, so the unification claim across paradigms is only superficially tested.

Correlation is a weak evaluation metric here. The scatter plots show highly polarized, roughly bimodal estimates (good vs. bad pretext tasks), so the reported Pearson coefficients (0.78-0.82) may largely reflect coarse separation rather than fine-grained predictive power—which is what pretext selection actually requires. No top-k selection accuracy or utility-based evaluation is reported. Correlations also degrade substantially in several conditions (ResNet-50 semi-supervised: 0.478; MoCo: 0.453; ImageNet-200: 0.675), which is described as robustness success without adequate discussion.

The Bearer [REDACTED] setting (ViT-B, 5 epochs, LR 5e-5, MSE consistency loss) is not representative of how SSL is actually practiced, and results under realistic algorithms show materially weaker and uneven correlations, weakening the practical significance of the method.

Presentation and completeness issues: broken cross-references ('??' for the Bearer [REDACTED] in the appendix), typographical errors ('reache', 'shown in table 1'), and the problem formulation assumes a logic-style satisfaction operator (|=) applied to neural predictions and augmentations that is never formally defined. No code or benchmark release is mentioned, limiting reproducibility given the large experimental matrix.

There is no limitations discussion, and the Impact Statement is boilerplate. The honest treatment of the observed failure modes (e.g., weak correlations under some algorithms/backbones) would substantially strengthen the paper.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored and practically important problem: estimating the benefit of a pretext task for a downstream target task *before* expensive training and validation. A reliable, cheap pretext-task selection method would reduce substantial trial-and-error cost in SSL/semi-supervised pipelines.

The conceptual decomposition of a pretext assumption into learnability (model), reliability (data), and completeness (target) is intuitive and connects SSL assumptions to knowledge-integrated learning and the NeSy shortcut problem in a potentially useful way, offering a new lens even if the formal results are loose.

The empirical coverage is broad: 115 pretext-task variants across three datasets, ablations showing each indicator contributes, and robustness checks over algorithms (MeanTeacher/UDA/FixMatch, SimCLR/MoCo/BYOL/DINO), backbones (ViT-B, ResNet-50), distribution shift (Office-31), data scale, and hyperparameters.

A cost comparison (Table 4) and a significance test against the critical Pearson coefficient provide concrete evidence that the estimation procedure is far cheaper than full training/validation and that observed correlations are statistically nonzero.
The benchmark of over one hundred pretext-task configurations (augmentation families x strength levels) is a potentially reusable community resource.
weaknesses: The theory is substantially weaker than claimed. The paper asserts a 'rigorous derivation,' but Eq. (8) is an informal upper bound built on an implicit independence assumption between the three error factors that is never justified. The definition of the three errors (Eqs. 2-8) mixes different distributions and conditioning events, and the probabilistic identity in Eq. (1) is heuristic rather than derived. Crucially, the theory yields only an upper bound on R_target, yet Eq. (17) uses the bound as a point estimate of target performance without any argument for why the estimate should be accurate or calibrated.

The empirical learnability indicator (Eq. 10) uses *training* error on a small sample as an estimate of generalization error on the pretext task, which contradicts the theoretical definition of R_unlearnable as a population quantity; this train/test inconsistency is not discussed.

The quantitative estimation claim is only partially supported. Scatter plots show a strongly polarized outcome distribution (good vs. bad tasks) with large within-cluster scatter; the method may effectively separate bad from good tasks rather than 'quantitatively estimate the actual target performance.' No ranking or selection metrics are reported (e.g., Spearman correlation, top-k retrieval accuracy), even though pretext *selection* is the stated motivating use case. Robustness correlations vary widely (0.478 for ResNet-50 semi-supervised; 0.453 for MoCo), which sits uneasily with the 'strongly correlates' claim in the abstract.

Missing baseline comparisons. The method trains both a pretext model and a supervised f_target on the small labeled set; natural cheap baselines — e.g., correlation of fine-tuned or linear-probe accuracy of f_target alone, or pretext-training loss alone (which the ablation suggests is weak, but only in isolation within the proposed framework) — are not evaluated, so the added value over simpler proxies is unclear. There is also a circularity concern: completeness is estimated by agreement with f_target, so part of the signal comes from the supervised model rather than from the assumption analysis.

Scope is narrow relative to the framing: all pretext tasks share the same augmentation-consistency assumption type, on image classification only. The claim that the framework covers SSL assumptions generally (rotation-invariance-style knowledge, etc.) is asserted but not tested beyond this family.

Presentation quality is below acceptance bar in places: broken cross-references ('settings described in ??'), duplicated/inconsistent captions in the appendix (CIFAR-100 figures labeled CIFAR-10, Office-31 text/figure setting mismatch), typos ('reache'), and the NeSy/knowledge-integration framing feels bolted on rather than load-bearing. No code release is mentioned, which harms reproducibility of a method whose value depends on implementation details (prototype matching, data selection procedures).

The 'low cost' advantage needs qualification: estimation still requires training a separate pretext model per task; the savings come from small data and few epochs, and the estimated performance is biased low relative to full training, so its usefulness for selecting near-optimal tasks (where differences are small) is not demonstrated.
